title: 道德經 第五十一章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 51, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 78. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 51 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 養德 (Nourishing Potency). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
道生之，
德畜之，
物形之，
勢成之。

sentences.l:
The Way gives them life,
potency rears them,
things give them shape,
circumstance completes them.
sentences.n:
Four clauses cut to one pattern — subject, verb, 之 'them' — and the chapter is built on the chain they make. 之 is the object pronoun here, not the 'of' it was in chapter 1; nothing on the page tells the two apart but position.

形 is the noun 'shape' pressed into service as a verb, with no ending to mark the change: 'things shape them'. Wang Bi runs the chain out plainly — what a thing lives by is the Way, what feeds it is potency, what gives it form is the things about it, what finishes it is the way circumstances stand. 勢 is that last word: not fate, but the lean a situation already has.

The Mawangdui silk manuscripts are read as writing 器 qì, 'a vessel, an implement', where ours has 勢 — which would make the finisher a thing made rather than a force at work.

sentences.t: 是以萬物莫不尊道而貴德。

sentences.l: Therefore among the ten-thousand things there is none that does not honour the Way and prize potency.
sentences.i: So every one of the ten thousand things honours the Way and holds potency precious.
sentences.n:
莫不 is a double negative doing the work of 'every one of them does'. 莫 is a negative pronoun that carries its own subject — 'there is none that' — so it needs no noun of its own; 萬物 standing in front of it is the topic, the set it ranges over.

尊 and 貴 are both adjectives ('exalted', 'costly') working as transitive verbs: to treat as exalted, to treat as costly. English has to reach for 'honour' and 'prize'; the Chinese simply puts the adjective where a verb goes.

道之尊，
德之貴，
夫莫之命而常自然。

sentences.l:
The Way's being honoured,
potency's being prized —
now, no one decrees it, and yet it is abidingly so of itself.
sentences.i: That the Way is honoured and potency prized: no one ordains it; it is always so of itself.
sentences.n:
之 turns up here in the third of its jobs, the one chapter 21's 道之為物 already showed. In chapter 1 it was 'of'; in the unit above it was 'them'; here it stands between a subject and its verb and makes the whole clause into a noun — 道之尊 is not 'the Way honours' but 'the Way's being honoured'. One character, three grammars, nothing to part them but where they sit.

莫之命 has the pronoun object in front of its verb, which is not the usual order. Classical Chinese moves a pronoun object forward when the clause is negated: 莫之命 for 莫命之. Chapter 53's 唯施是畏 fronts an object too, but by a different device: there a particle 是 is left standing in the empty place.

自然 is fixed in our English as 'so of itself'. It is not yet 'nature' — that sense came later; here it is exactly what the two characters say, self-so.

sentences.l:
Therefore the Way gives them life,
potency rears them.
Raises them, nurses them,
steadies them, ripens them,
covers them, shelters them.
sentences.i: So the Way gives them life and potency feeds them: brings them up and nurses them, steadies them and ripens them, keeps them and covers them over.
sentences.n:
長 is zhǎng here, 'to bring on to growth', not the cháng 'long' of chapters 44 and 54 — the trap chapter 10 already sprang once.

亭之毒之 is a real crux. On their face the characters are 'a post-house' and 'poison', which is nonsense in a list of kindnesses, so the tradition reads them as loan-writings for other words: 亭 for 定 'to settle' and 毒 for 篤 'to make solid' or 熟 'to ripen'. The pair 亭毒 later hardened into a standing phrase for bringing a thing to maturity, and it is read tíng dú, which is why the pinyin here gives the graphs their own sound. We are following a guess that is very old and very widely shared, not a certainty.

蓋 is the plain verb 'to cover' here. In chapter 50 the same character was the particle 'as one hears it' — that particle grew out of this image, a thatch laid over a thing.

生而不有，
為而不恃，

sentences.l:
Gives life and yet does not possess,
acts and yet does not presume on it,
sentences.n:
You have met these lines twice: chapter 2 had the first two, chapter 10 all four. The repetition is the text's, not ours.

What is new is the subject. In chapter 10 it was left open; here the four units before it have named it outright — the Way, and the potency that feeds what the Way begets.

長而不宰。
是謂玄德。

sentences.l:
brings them on and yet does not master them.
This is called dark potency.
sentences.n:
是謂 is the book's naming formula: the demonstrative 是 as subject, 謂 as verb, and no copula anywhere in it — 是 is never the verb 'to be' in this language, however much it looks like the modern one.

玄德 stays two words, here and in chapter 10: a modifier and its noun that mean just what their parts mean, unlike 玄牝 in chapter 6, which the text christens outright. 玄 is not evil-dark. It is the colour of deep water.
